blanks.subject: Bank of Korea — its own list of currency swap arrangements is complete in the file
blanks.text: The Bank of Korea's page 'Currency Swap — Current Status of the Bank of Korea's Currency Swap Arrangements' (bok.or.kr, International Relations section) was fetched with curl and read in full as raw text. Its table, headed 'as of the end of March 2026', has exactly nine bilateral columns plus one multilateral column: Canada (no pre-set total principal amount), China 70 trillion KRW / 400 billion CNY, Switzerland 11.2 trillion KRW / 10 billion CHF, Indonesia 10.7 trillion KRW / 115 trillion IDR, Japan 10 billion USD, Australia 9.6 trillion KRW / 12 billion AUD, UAE 6.1 trillion KRW / 20 billion AED, Malaysia 5 trillion KRW / 15 billion MYR, Türkiye 2.3 trillion KRW / 56 billion TRY, and the CMIM at 38.4 billion USD; the page gives the total as approximately 150.6 billion USD excluding Canada. Every one of those ten is already filed, with amounts that match. The table gives maturities only (Canada none, China Oct.2025, Switzerland Mar.2026, Indonesia Mar.2026, Japan Nov.2026, Australia Feb.2028, UAE Apr.2027, Malaysia May.2027, Türkiye Aug.2027, CMIM none) and no signing dates, so the null signed_or_renewed on the filed Korea-UAE record cannot be closed from this page. The Bank of Korea is exhausted as a provider at the counterparty level.

blanks.subject: Chiang Mai Initiative Multilateralisation — already complete in the file, so no fetch was spent on AMRO
blanks.text: Before fetching anything I listed every record in agents/swaps.json with kind 'multilateral'. All fourteen CMIM participants are already filed from the AMRO Factsheet 2026, each with its financial contribution and maximum arrangement amount: China 68.4/34.2, Hong Kong 8.4/8.4, Japan 76.8/38.4, Korea 38.4 (total principal amount, from the Bank of Korea table), Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and the Philippines at 9.104/22.76 each, Vietnam 2/10, Cambodia 0.24/1.2, Myanmar 0.12/0.6, Brunei 0.06/0.3 and Laos 0.06/0.3 (USD billions). Japan's CMIM amendment dates of 2009-12-28, 2010-03-24, 2014-07-17, 2020-06-23 and 2021-03-31 are filed as well, along with Japan's seven bilateral swap arrangements with Indonesia, India, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Task 2 of this assignment was therefore already done before the round began, and the budget went to the supply side that was genuinely missing. Nothing was re-fetched from AMRO.

blanks.subject: Reserve Bank of India — no SAARC bilateral swap agreement with Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan or Afghanistan has been published
blanks.text: The RBI's own International Relations press-release archive (FS_PressRelease.aspx?fn=2779) was fetched with curl and read in full as raw text, including the embedded link table. It carries exactly seven press releases, and the swap ones are: Maldives 7 October 2024, the SAARC framework 27 June 2024, Maldives 8 December 2022, Sri Lanka 27 July 2020, the SAARC framework 26 November 2019, and Sri Lanka 29 March 2016. There is no press release for Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan or Afghanistan, and none for Bhutan on this list either. Both framework releases say the facility 'will be available to all SAARC member countries, subject to their signing the bilateral swap agreements' — that is a mechanism, not a signed agreement, so no member was filed on membership alone. The only Bhutan record in the file remains the expired 2016 one sourced to Business Standard; the RBI has published nothing on Bhutan under the 2024-27 framework that this archive shows.

blanks.subject: Swiss National Bank — its own Q&A page read in full, three records out of it, nothing else there
blanks.text: The SNB's 'Questions and answers on foreign exchange swaps in Swiss francs' page was fetched with curl and read in full as raw text (about 18,000 characters). It names every swap arrangement the SNB says it has ever had with another central bank: the US Federal Reserve, the six-central-bank network of the Bank of Canada, the Bank of England, the Bank of Japan, the ECB, the Fed and the SNB, made standing in October 2013; the National Bank of Belgium 'put into place many years ago'; the National Bank of Poland, June 2012; the central bank of China, July 2014; the Bank of Korea, February 2018; and the EUR/CHF arrangements with the ECB, the National Bank of Poland and the Hungarian central bank under which the SNB supplied Swiss francs from October 2008 to January 2010. Of those, Hungary, the ECB-side Swiss-franc arrangement and the February 2018 Korea signing were not in the file and are filed this round. The rest are already filed, mostly from the other side. The page gives no amount for any arrangement except in passing (the largest weekly US dollar allocation of USD 11.1 billion in October 2022, which is a drawing, not a line size), so no amount was recorded for the three new records.

blanks.subject: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye — no counterparty beyond the five already filed
blanks.text: A search of CBRT swap announcements returned coverage of only four counterparties: South Korea (the renewal already filed from the Korean side), the UAE (filed, 2 October 2025 and the expired January 2022 line), Qatar (filed 2020 and the December 2021 extension, with the 18 August 2018 original filed this round from the Qatari side) and China (filed). Kazakhstan is filed from a CBRT announcement already. The CBRT's own press-release index at tcmb.gov.tr/wps/wcm/connect/EN/TCMB+EN/Main+Menu/Announcements/Press+Releases was fetched with curl and returned an 11 KB navigation shell with no press-release listing and no occurrence of the word 'swap' — a quiet 200, so the index itself was not actually tested. No new CBRT counterparty was evidenced.

blanks.subject: Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) — no swap line other than the PBoC one
blanks.text: A search for SAMA bilateral currency swap agreements returned nothing but the November 2023 CNY 50 billion / SAR 26 billion agreement with the People's Bank of China, which is already filed, reported identically by Arab News, SCMP, Saudi Gazette, Argaam and others, with SAMA's own announcement at sama.gov.sa/en-US/News/Pages/news-994.aspx (not opened this round). SAMA appears in this row only as a counterparty of the PBoC, with no line of its own as provider. Not a document-level blank: SAMA's own publications index was not opened, so this rests on the search returning no other counterparty.

blanks.subject: IMF Working Paper 2021/210, 'Evolution of Bilateral Swap Lines' — the one document that would give a full cross-provider denominator
blanks.text: This paper builds a database of bilateral swap lines and its appendix tables list China's roughly 37 counterparties and Japan's ten arrangements with signing dates and amounts. Both PDF paths — imf.org/-/media/Files/Publications/WP/2021/English/wpiea2021210-print-pdf.ashx and the .pdf form the publication page gives — return HTTP 403 to curl with a browser user-agent, and the fetch tool returns only a summariser's prose, which this project does not accept as evidence for an amount or a date. So the paper's tables have not been read and no record or denominator entry rests on them. What the summary did flag, and what a future round should test against a primary source, is that the paper counts UAE lines with India and Korea, and that it treats Japan's Ministry of Finance arrangements as swap lines even though the MoF is a finance ministry rather than a central bank — which matters for this row's rule about arrangements that lend to governments.

blanks.subject: A CBUAE-Reserve Bank of India currency swap
blanks.text: The IMF paper's summary and a Gulf News report point to a UAE-India central bank 'currency swap MoU' signed around 2018. A memorandum of understanding to enter into a swap names a mechanism and is not evidence that a swap agreement exists, which this project's rules refuse, and the RBI's own International Relations press-release archive — read in full this round — contains no UAE release at all. Nothing was filed. The thing that would settle it is a CBUAE press release of the kind that exists for Bahrain, Egypt, Ethiopia, Türkiye and China.

blanks.subject: CBUAE memoranda of understanding with Bank Indonesia on local-currency settlement
blanks.text: The CBUAE has published two MoUs with Bank Indonesia, one 'to promote the use of national currencies for bilateral trade' and one on payments cooperation. Neither is a swap or repo line between the two central banks, and a local-currency settlement framework is the same category of thing round 76 refused when it rejected a trade-settlement clearing union. Nothing was filed for Indonesia from the UAE side. The same reasoning applies to the two MoUs that accompany the Ethiopia swap: only the swap itself was recorded.

blanks.subject: Bank of England, Bank of Canada and Reserve Bank of Australia as providers beyond what is filed
blanks.text: No publication of any of the three was opened this round. What is already filed for them is the six-central-bank standing network of 31 October 2013, each one's renminbi line from the PBoC side, the Bank of Canada's unlimited line with the Bank of Korea of 15 November 2017, and the Reserve Bank of Australia's Indonesian line of 4 March 2025 with its expired 2022 predecessor. Whether any of the three has a further counterparty has therefore not actually been tested, and a future round should open the Bank of England's and the Reserve Bank of Australia's own swap-arrangement pages rather than relying on the Fed network to stand in for them.

checked_not_in_assignment.text: The same PBoC page that supports this round's status updates states: 'As of September 30, 2025, the People's Bank of China (PBoC) has signed bilateral local currency swap agreements with the central banks or monetary authorities of 32 countries and regions. The outstanding balance of RMB drawn by overseas central banks or monetary authorities stands at RMB 79.3 billion.' That is a system-level figure about how much of the network is actually in use, which no record in this row carries, and it may be worth a note on the map rather than a record.

Still worth settling whether FLAR lends to central banks or to member states, because if it lends to finance ministries the six existing FLAR records are in the same category round 76 refused for the Arab Monetary Fund.
